01: Amtrak runs its first trains, taking over intercity passenger service from 20 railroads. Of 366 train routes running the day before, it keeps 184.
02: The United States switches off 'Selective Availability', the deliberate blurring of the civilian GPS signal. Receivers go from about 100 meters of error to about 5.
03: A Digital Equipment marketer sends an ad for a computer demonstration to about 400 ARPANET users at once: the first spam e-mail. He is made to promise not to do it again.
04: A U.S. Army lieutenant is handed the keys to the French canal works in Panama, and the American effort begins. The Panama Canal opened to ships on August 15, 1914.
05: Alan Shepard rides Freedom 7, a Mercury capsule built by McDonnell Aircraft, 116 miles up on a 15-minute flight: the first American in space.
06: The airship Hindenburg burns while landing at Lakehurst, New Jersey. Of 97 aboard, 35 die, and one man on the ground. Radio reporter Herbert Morrison's recording carries the words 'Oh, the humanity.'
Queen Elizabeth II and President Mitterrand open the Channel Tunnel: 31 miles of railway between England and France, 23.5 of them under the sea.
07: In St. Petersburg, Alexander Popov presents his lightning detector, a receiver that rings a bell when it picks up the radio pulse of a distant strike. Russia keeps May 7 as Radio Day.
The German submarine U-20 torpedoes the liner Lusitania off the Old Head of Kinsale, Ireland. She sinks in 18 minutes; 1,197 of the 1,960 aboard die, about 128 of them Americans.
08: The Smith-Lever Act creates the Cooperative Extension Service, sending the land-grant colleges' know-how out to farm families.
V-E Day: Germany's surrender takes effect and the war in Europe is over. It is President Truman's 61st birthday; he was born in Lamar, Missouri, in 1884.
09: British escorts force the submarine U-110 to the surface, and a boarding party from HMS Bulldog carries off her Enigma machine and code books. The capture is kept secret.
10: At Promontory Summit, Utah, Leland Stanford drives the last spike joining the Central Pacific and Union Pacific. The telegraph flashes one word across the country: DONE.
11: A dust storm that rose off the Great Plains two days earlier reaches New York, Boston and Washington. On the way it dropped 12 million pounds of dust on Chicago.
In New York, IBM's Deep Blue wins the sixth game and the match, 3.5 to 2.5: the first time a computer beats a reigning world chess champion, Garry Kasparov, in a match.
12: In Berlin, Konrad Zuse presents the Z3, built from 2,600 relays: the first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer. Bombing destroyed it in 1943.
13: The first Formula One world championship race is run at Silverstone, England, with King George VI watching. Nino Farina wins in an Alfa Romeo.
14: William Clark and about 30 men set out from Camp Dubois, Illinois, and start up the Missouri River: the Lewis and Clark Expedition is under way.
15: President Lincoln signs the law creating the U.S. Department of Agriculture. He called it 'the people's department.'
16: The Dambusters: 19 Lancasters of No. 617 Squadron under Guy Gibson fly to Germany with Barnes Wallis's bouncing bombs and breach the Mohne and Eder dams. Eight aircraft do not return.
17: A college baseball game in New York, Columbia against Princeton, is the first sporting event shown on television in the United States.
18: Jacqueline Cochran, flying a Canadair Sabre over Rogers Dry Lake, California, becomes the first woman to break the sound barrier. Chuck Yeager had encouraged her.
19: New England's Dark Day: the sky goes so dark that candles are needed from noon. Forest-fire smoke, fog and cloud were to blame; many feared the Day of Judgment.
20: Charles Lindbergh takes off from New York in the Spirit of St. Louis, paid for by St. Louis backers. He lands in Paris the next day, 3,600 miles and more than 33 hours later.
21: Amelia Earhart lands her Lockheed Vega near Derry, Northern Ireland, 14 hours 56 minutes out of Newfoundland: the first woman to fly the Atlantic alone.
22: Abraham Lincoln is granted U.S. patent 6,469 for inflatable bladders to float a steamboat over shoals. He is the only president to hold a patent.
Microsoft releases Windows 3.0, the first version of Windows to win wide acclaim. It sold about 10 million copies.
23: The submarine USS Squalus sinks on a test dive off New Hampshire in 243 feet of water. Twenty-six men die; divers bring up all 33 survivors with the new McCann rescue chamber.
24: Samuel Morse opens his telegraph line with a message from Washington to Baltimore: 'What hath God wrought.'
25: President Kennedy asks Congress to commit the nation to 'landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth' before the decade is out.
26: Henry Ford and his son Edsel drive the 15-millionth Model T out of the factory, and the car's long run comes to an end.
Operation Dynamo begins at Dunkirk. By June 4 a fleet of more than 800 vessels, many of them small civilian boats, has brought 338,226 Allied soldiers back across the Channel.
27: About 6:30 p.m. a tornado cuts a mile-wide path through St. Louis, crosses the Mississippi at the Eads Bridge and strikes East St. Louis. At least 255 people are killed.
The German battleship Bismarck is sunk in the Atlantic by the Royal Navy, three days after she sank HMS Hood. Of more than 2,200 men aboard, 114 survive.
28: Volkswagen is founded in Berlin by the German Labour Front. The name means 'people's car.'
29: In fog on the St. Lawrence River the liner Empress of Ireland is rammed by the collier Storstad and sinks in 14 minutes. Of 1,477 aboard, 1,012 die.
30: Ray Harroun wins the first Indianapolis 500 in the Marmon Wasp at 74.6 miles per hour. He drives alone, with a rear-view mirror in place of a riding mechanic.
31: After a day of heavy rain the South Fork Dam gives way above Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The flood kills 2,208. Clara Barton's Red Cross stays more than five months.
